beats.text: Algebra and algorithm both come from the same person.
beats.note: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, a scholar working in Baghdad in the ninth century.

beats.name: Al-Khwarizmi
beats.role: Wrote 'al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wal-muqabala', 'The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing'.

beats.text: 'Al-jabr', part of that title, meant completing or rejoining broken parts. Carried into Latin, it became 'algebra'.
beats.note: The book's method for solving equations is what made the title worth borrowing.

beats.text: When 12th-century translators rendered his name in Latin, they wrote it as 'Algoritmi'.
beats.note: That Latinised name became the root of 'algorithm', through a later translation of his separate work on Hindu-Arabic numerals.

beats.text: He used neither word himself. Translators built both out of his name and his title, centuries after he wrote them.

beats.line: Algebra and algorithm: one man, one book.
